metadata.title: Language exposure and English digital reading achievement in East Asia: Examining the role of students’ socioeconomic status

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for English digital reading, restricting the analytic sample to students who completed the reading assessment in English in Macao, Hong Kong, and Singapore (total n=7,703). The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling weights or replicate weights were applied, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or describe complex survey variance estimation. Because the analysis is conducted in SPSS using Pearson correlations and hierarchical linear regression, the paper does not document a weighting strategy consistent with PISA’s complex sampling design. As a result, readers should treat the reported associations as descriptive/associational estimates that may be sensitive to the omission of survey-weighted estimation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 data and selected students from Macao, Hong Kong, and Singapore who completed the reading assessment in English via computers. The dependent variable was the PISA 2018 plausible value PV1READ (English digital reading). Missing values were handled using MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS before conducting Pearson correlations and hierarchical linear regression models.

main_findings.performance_metrics: Hierarchical linear regression (SPSS): Model 1 r2=0.14, SES β=0.38***; Model 2 r2=0.22, SES β=0.313***, LE-mother β=-0.03*, LE-father β=-0.00 (ns), LE-siblings β=0.12***, LE-friend β=0.16***, LE-schoolmates β=0.08***. Model 3 moderation terms (SES*language exposure) all insignificant (e.g., SES*LE-mother β=0.05, SES*LE-friend β=0.01).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 English digital reading data (PV1READ), the study leveraged socioeconomic status (ESCS) and language exposure from parents and peers (mother, father, siblings, best friends, schoolmates) to predict English digital reading achievement, finding that SES had a significant positive association while parental language exposure from mother showed a small negative effect and peer language exposures (siblings and best friends) showed positive effects. This indicates that improving students’ socioeconomic resources and supporting high-quality peer/family language interactions may be more actionable than relying on SES to buffer the language-exposure–reading link, though the study’s correlational design and single-PV outcome limit causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: This study used PISA 2018 microdata for English digital reading, restricting the sample to students who took the computer-based reading assessment in English in Macao (n=679), Hong Kong (n=348), and Singapore (n=6,676), for a total of 7,703 students. The dependent variable was the PISA plausible value PV1READ, and missing data were addressed via MCMC multiple imputation in SPSS. Pearson correlations showed positive associations between SES and English digital reading in all three economies (whole sample r=0.38, p<0.01), while language exposure–reading correlations varied by source and economy. In hierarchical linear regression, SES significantly predicted reading achievement (whole sample Model 1 r2=0.14, β=0.38***), and in Model 2 SES remained significant (r2=0.22, β=0.313***), with LE-mother showing a small negative effect (β=-0.03*, p<0.05) and peer exposures such as siblings (β=0.12***) and best friends (β=0.16***) showing positive effects. The moderation tests in Model 3 indicated that SES did not significantly moderate the language exposure–reading relationship, and the manuscript does not report survey-weighted estimation, limiting generalizability and causal claims.
